rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form and root occur only here in the Quran.
rows.anchor: وحيدة فى القرآن صيغة ومادة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tactile gloss of smooth requires hardness and barrenness; smoothness alone does not make something ṣald.
rows.anchor: تأويلها بالملامسة يحتاج إلى قيد بالصلابة والجدب، فليس كل أملس صلدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word usually describes stone or hard barren ground, then extends to stinginess, an unproductive flint, and a she-camel withholding milk.
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما يستعمل فى الحجر وفى الأرض الصلداء الغليظة الصلبة، ونقل إلى الشحِّ والضنِّ

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari defines ṣald stone as hard and bare of plants or anything else, and ṣald land as infertile; he says exegetes agree.
rows.anchor: قال الطبرى: والصلد من الحجارة: الصلب الذى لا شيء عليه من نبات ولا غيره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem applies ṣald to an ancestral stronghold; editions K and T add the gloss smooth, with nothing upon it.
rows.anchor: لآباء صدق مجدهم معقل صلد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses ghayr mamnun as undiminished and says Arabs use the word this way, citing Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: غير منقوص. ولما سأله ابن الأزرق: وهل تعرف العرب ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣafwān occurs in this form only once in the Quran.
rows.anchor: وحيدة الصيغة فى القرآن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lexicographers differ on whether ṣafwān is one ṣafwāna or the singular of ṣafī.
rows.anchor: والصفوان قيل واحدة صفوانة، وقيل هو واحد الصفِىّ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same root appears in Quranic forms of choosing, in the participles al-muṣṭafayn al-akhyār and ʿasal muṣaffā, and in al-Ṣafā.
rows.anchor: وفعل الاصطفاء ماضيا ومضارعا اثني عشرة مرة، واسم المفعولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading ṣald as a smooth stone makes the parable say dew strikes a smooth stone and leaves it smooth; she says this reading is unconvincing.
rows.anchor: فكان تأويل الآية عنده: كمثل حجبر أملس أصابه طل فتركه حجرا أملس. ولا يبدو قريبا.

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives ṣafā from purity, freedom from admixture; ṣafwān is like ṣafā, with ṣafwāna as its singular, and may describe a clear sunny day that is very cold.
rows.anchor: أن أصل الصفاء خلوص الشيء من الشوب. ومنه الصفا للحجارة الصافية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dictionaries also define ṣafwān as a large, solid stone on which nothing grows, and record related forms for a hen that stops laying and a man free of something.
rows.anchor: وتذكر المعاجم فى صفوانٍ: الحجر الصلد الضخم لا ينبت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains ghayr mamnun as an undiminished reward and cites Zuhayr’s line about a generous man who does not give a grudging or capricious gift.
rows.anchor: فلا. . . يُعْطِي بذلك مَمْنُوْناً ولا نَزِقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase occurs in the Quranic reward passages in al-Qalam, Fussilat, al-Inshiqaq, and al-Tin; the root mann occurs sixteen times, as does the phrase r-rayb al-manun in al-Tur.
rows.anchor: ومعها (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ) فى آيات.

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari glosses the phrase as neither diminished nor cut off, connecting it with the word for a fraying rope.
rows.anchor: فسَّره الطبرى كذلك، بغير منقوص ولامقطوع، من قولهم: حبل مَنِين.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra glosses it as uncut; Arabic also uses the root for strength failing and for a weak person.
rows.anchor: وفي معنى الكلمة عند الفراء: غير مقطوع، والعربُ تقول ضعفت منتى عن السفر.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the reward as uncounted.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: غير محسوب.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the reward as unclouded by reminders of generosity.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: غير مكدرٍ بالمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation is that the reward is not measured.
rows.anchor: وقيل: غير مقدر.

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi distinguishes measured recompense from unmeasured grace: reward is assessed, whereas divine favor is not.
rows.anchor: وهو التفضل لأن الجزاء مقدر والفضل غير مقدر. ذكره الماوردى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads it as a reward not bestowed as a favor, since it is due for the Prophet’s work; he says favors, unlike earned rewards, may be held over someone.
rows.anchor: غير ممنون به عليك، لأنه ثواب تستوجبه على عملك وليس بتفضل ابتداء

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects al-Zamakhshari’s reading as carrying a Muʿtazilite implication.
rows.anchor: أنكره أبو حيان ورأى فيها دسيسة اعتزال

rows.speaker: ناصر الدين ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munir condemns al-Zamakhshari’s claim: the Prophet’s hadith says no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, but by God’s grace and mercy.
rows.anchor: لا يدخل أحدكم الجنة بعمله

rows.speaker: خالد بن صفوان
rows.claim: Khalid ibn Safwan asks how later Arabs could compete with the first eloquent Arabs when they only imitate their predecessors and inherit their linguistic stock.
rows.anchor: كيف نجاريهم وإنما نحكيهم؟ أم كيف نسابقهم وإنما نجري على ما سبق إلينا من أعراقهم؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first generation’s inability to answer the Quranic challenge is decisive evidence, because they possessed the deepest command of the language in which it was revealed.
rows.anchor: عجز البلغاء من العصر الأول، عن معارضة القرآن، وفيهم أصل الفصاحة، برهان قاطع في قضية التحدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge’s decisive result in the Prophet’s era does not confine the Quran’s inimitability to that era; those Arabs were addressed as the language’s experts, and could not produce a surah like it.
rows.anchor: اختصاصهم بالتحدي جاء من كونهم أهل الاختصاص بالعربية لغة القرآن، وقد حسمها عجزهم عن أن يأتوا بسورة من مثله

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the Quran’s miracle endures through all days and ages.
rows.anchor: كما قال الإمام الطبري في مقدمة تفسيره

rows.speaker: نافع بن الأزرق
rows.claim: Nafi ibn al-Azraq and Najda ibn Uwaymir confronted Ibn Abbas over his Quranic interpretation and legal opinions, asking him for Arabic usage as evidence; Ibn Abbas invited their questions.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: سلاني عما بدا لكما

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti reports that the collection contains 190 questions and that he omitted about fourteen; imams had also transmitted individual questions to Ibn Abbas through different routes.
rows.anchor: قال السيوطي بعد أن ساقها

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says Ibn al-Anbari preserved a marked selection in Kitab al-Waqf wa-l-Ibtida, while al-Tabarani included another selection in al-Muʿjam al-Kabir through Juwaybir from al-Dahhak.
rows.anchor: وخرج الطبراني في (معجمه الكبير) منه قطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati says she could not obtain the old copy identified by its colored marks and letter symbols; she begins to note al-Hurayni’s warning about locating it.
rows.anchor: ولم تصل إلينا النسخة العتيقة المعلم بالحمرة وحرف كُ على المنقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farra, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Tabrizi, and lexicons attest that sariy means a small river or stream; in Maryam it is one of several interpretations.
rows.anchor: تفسير السرى بالنهر الصغير، والجدول هو المعروف من كلام العرب

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Hasan recited the verse and said Maryam’s child was a sariy; Khalid ibn Safwan clarified that Arabs call a stream sariy, and al-Hasan agreed.
rows.anchor: فأسند عن الحسن - البصري، أبي سعيد - انه تلا الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form is unique in the Quran; related forms occur in the night-travel verb, the Prophet’s Night Journey, and commands to Lot and Moses to travel by night.
rows.anchor: ومعها من مادتها جاء فِعل السُّرى مضارعاً في آية الفجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says sealing and stamping hearts are metaphors for deeply rooted heedlessness and misguidance, with sealing suggesting closure and finality beyond its literal sense.
rows.anchor: رسوخ الغفلة والضلال، وراء معناه القريب فى الختم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari interprets the earlier phrase as God stamping hearts; the author notes that Quranic uses of stamping occur in contexts of disbelievers, hypocrites, transgressors, and tyrants.
rows.anchor: وتأويلها فى المسألة: طبع على قلوبهم، نحو ما قاله الطبرى فى تأويله

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib rejects the view that God places a literal sensory seal on disbelievers’ hearts as a sign to angels: anatomy would reveal it, or angels already know their beliefs.
rows.anchor: وليس ذلك بشيء، فإن هذه الكناية إن كانت محسوسة، فمن حقها أن يدركها أصحاب التشريح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses ṣafwān as a smooth stone and cites a line by Aws ibn Hajar.
rows.anchor: فقال: الحجر الأملس. واستشهد بقول. أوس بن حجر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses marāghaman as an open, spacious place in the Hudhayl dialect and supports the gloss with poetry.
rows.anchor: ومثله تأويل الطبرى للكلمة، ثم أسند عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marāghaman occurs only once in both form and root in the Quran.
rows.anchor: وحيدة فى القرآن صيغة ومادة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spaciousness is not a primary sense of the word; it is inferred from its coordination with wasaʿatan.
rows.anchor: وليس الانفساح من معانيها القريبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root begins with dust and humiliation, extends to coercion, then shifts to a place of escape or refuge, as mafzaʿ is refuge from fear.
rows.anchor: وأصل استعمالها لغة الرغام التراب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra calls marāgham and murāghama verbal nouns and glosses marāgham as a place of movement or destination in the land.
rows.anchor: فالمراغم المضطرب والمذهب فى الأرض

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari gives a similar interpretation and reports Ibn Abbas as saying it means traveling from one land to another, al-Dahhak as saying changing place, and others as moving away.
rows.anchor: المراغم المتجول من الأرض إلى الأرض، وعن الضحاك

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains it as a place one goes to when confronted with something objectionable, analogizing expressions for going to someone out of anger or complaint.
rows.anchor: أي مذهبا يذهب إليه إذا رأى منكرا يلزمه أن يغضب منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suggests marāghaman conveys the forced character of migration as well as the spaciousness of the land.
rows.anchor: مع سعة فى الأرض، إرغام الاضطرار إلى الهجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the cited poem, mann comes explicitly from bi-mannihi, not from the phrase thumma akda.
rows.anchor: وإنما يؤخذ من صريح قوله * بمنَّه *

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib treats akda as a small gift, but the author argues that its coordination with “gave a little” requires a distinct meaning.
rows.anchor: فلزم أن يكون هناك فرق بين الإكداء وإعطاء القليل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra glosses akda as holding back after giving a little; Arabic idiom uses the word for stopping after a gift.
rows.anchor: ومعناه عند الفراء: أمسك بعد عطاء قليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers stinginess after a small gift, linked to encountering hard ground while digging; this does not require the extra idea of spoiling a gift with reminders.
rows.anchor: البخل والشح بعد عطاء قليل. دون قيده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains wazar as a refuge and cites poetry by Ṭābin al-Dathniya as Arabic evidence.
rows.anchor: قال: الوزر الملجأ. قال: وهل كانت العرب تعرف ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sense of grazing occurs here alone; related forms in the Quran include other verbs and the words for marked and signs.
rows.anchor: ولم تأت الكلمة في هذا المعنى إلا هنا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Tabari gloss the word as grazing livestock; al-Tabari reports no disagreement among exegetes.
rows.anchor: وفي الطبري: ترعون، وأسنده عن أهل التأويل، لم يذكر

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib treats going in pursuit of something as the root sense, extended to grazing, seeking or inflicting punishment, and bargaining.
rows.anchor: أن أصل السوم الذهاب في ابتغاء الشيء

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir explains a hadith against grazing livestock before sunrise, and another saying that an animal grazing freely causes injury without liability.
rows.anchor: يعني أن الدابة المرسلة في مرعاها إذا أصابت أحداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grazing is the immediate sense here; the author connects punishment with sending out animals to pasture or horses to raid, with the object determining whether the sense is grazing, raiding, or oppression.
rows.anchor: والرعي هو المعنى المتبادر للسوم في الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿṣār occurs in this form only once; related Quranic forms are found in the two verses in Yusuf, al-Nabaʾ, and al-ʿAsr.
rows.anchor: الفعل من العصر فى آيتى يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe-wind interpretation fits the root’s sense of pressure and extraction; the word can also name a rising dust column or a wind driving clouds.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الإعصار بالريح الشديدة، قريب، مع ملحظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines iʿṣār as a wind that raises dust like a pillar or raises a thundercloud; al-Tabari gives the same gloss.
rows.anchor: الإعصار ريح تهب تثير الغبار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports Ibn Abbas interpreting it as a fierce wind carrying scorching heat, including the hot samum.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: هى السموم الحارة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines iʿṣār as a wind that stirs dust.
rows.anchor: وعند الراغب: الإعصار ريح تثير الغبار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses marāghaman as a spacious place in the Hudhayl dialect and cites a poem.
rows.anchor: بلغة هذيل. واستشهد له بقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi cite the poem for the interpretation of iqtirāf as accusation or claim.
rows.anchor: وهو من شواهد الطبرى والقرطبي، لقول من قال إن الاقتراف التهمة والادعاء

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit places qarf under accusation: qirti means my suspect, and qār afa something by encountering or committing it.
rows.anchor: فلان قِرتي، أي تُهمتى وقارَف شيئاً

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan restricts iqtirāf in the verse of al-Anʿam to sins.
rows.anchor: إلى تقييد الاقتراف، فى آية الأنعام، بالآثام

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris gives kasb the root sense of pursuing and acquiring, while q-r-f concerns contact and attachment, deriving from a peel that covers something.
rows.anchor: أصل صحيح يدل على ابتغاء وطلب وإصابة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives acquisition metaphorically from peeling bark or skin; it may be good or bad but is more often used for wrongdoing, and qaraftu can mean accused.
rows.anchor: أصل القرف والاقتراف: قشر اللحاء عن الشجر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The cited hadith tells people who complained of a place’s epidemic to move away, since contact with the disease can lead to death.
rows.anchor: تحولوا، فإن من القرَف التلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explaining dhi mirrah as strength in God’s command is an approximation: Arabic uses repeated twisting of rope to make it firm, then extends firmness metaphorically, as sabr extends from a bitter plant to endurance.
rows.anchor: هو من قبيل الشرح والتقريب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the clouds press one another so water emerges between them, citing a line by al-Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan.
rows.anchor: السحاب يعصر بعضها بعضاً فيخرج الماء من بين السحابتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form is unique in the Quran; its root also appears in al-ʿAsr, Yusuf’s dream and the harvest year, and the whirlwind in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وحيدة الصيغة في القرآن.

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir defines banān as the fingers or their tips; banāna is the singular.
rows.anchor: البنان الأصابع، وقيل أطرافها، واحدتها بنانة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says banān are the fingers as the body’s extremities and last parts to form, or that God can restore their finely detailed joints exactly as before.
rows.anchor: ذكر الأطراف على أنها أصابع الإنسان التى هى أطرافه وآخر ما يتم من خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported reading is that God can gather human bones yet make fingers and toes into a single hoof-like piece, preventing ordinary dexterity.
rows.anchor: عظام الإنسان - ونحن قادرون على أن

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls al-Zamakhshari’s wording affected; he reads the verse as restoring the fingers, among the most finely divided bones, at resurrection.
rows.anchor: ورأى أبو حيان فى قول الزمخشرى تكلفا وتنميق ألفاظ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and most exegetes say the fingers could be made into one lump or bone during life, diminishing their usefulness; the author says the resurrection reading is the clear intent.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول فيه توعد. والمعنى الأول هو الظاهر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses iʿṣār as a fierce wind; the cited poem describes a whirlwind and some editions add that it carries punishment.
rows.anchor: الريح الشديدة. واستشهد له بقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author treats the two-cloud explanation as a gloss, not a necessary restriction; rain clouds squeezed by rain are sufficient, and al-Raghib likewise does not require two clouds.
rows.anchor: ولا نرى ضرورة لقيد المعصرات بسحابتين

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines muʿṣirāt as rain-saturated clouds, while also reporting the alternative that they bring a whirlwind; the author rejects the latter from the verse’s context and Quranic usage.
rows.anchor: لم يحدد سحابتين، بل فسر المعصرات بالسحائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All forms of ʿaṣr derive from pressure to extract juice: pressing grapes, the press and its place, rain clouds yielding water, and iʿṣār as a strong wind driving clouds.
rows.anchor: والعصر في كل صيغة واستعماله، يرجع إلى أصل دلالته على الضغط لاستخلاص العصارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author derives ʿasr meaning time from human life being pressed through trials and hardship; she rejects al-Raghib’s derivation from what remains after squeezing.
rows.anchor: ملحوظ فيه أنه يستخلص عصارة الإنسان بالضغط والابتلاء والمعاناة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses ʿaḍud as a helper and supporter, citing a line by al-Nabigha.
rows.anchor: المعين الناصر، واستشهد بقول نابغة بني ذبيان
